items.prompt: Why are your fingers so slim, given how much force they can grip with?

options.label: Finger bones are hollow, unlike bones elsewhere in the body
options.feedback: There is nothing specially hollow about finger bones; the slimness comes from what tissue is, and isn't, packed inside the finger.

options.label: The muscles that move the fingers sit up in the forearm; only their tendons reach into the fingers themselves
options.feedback: Keeping the bulky muscle back in the forearm and pulling the finger from a distance is exactly what keeps the finger itself slim.

options.label: Fingers do not need much force, so little muscle is needed there
options.feedback: A gripping hand can exert real force; the force is generated elsewhere and simply delivered by cable-like tendons.

options.label: Tight skin over the fingers makes them look slimmer than they are
options.feedback: The slimness is not an illusion of the skin; there genuinely is very little muscle bulk inside a finger.

items.ok_line: The muscle stays in the forearm; only a tendon reaches the finger.
items.ko_title: Not about the bone or skin
items.ko_line: What keeps a finger slim is what's missing inside it, not its bone or its skin.
items.exp_text: The strength behind a gripping hand comes mostly from muscles bundled together in the forearm, not from anything inside the fingers themselves. Long tendons run from those muscles, cross the wrist, and thread into each finger, so pulling on a tendon from a distance is what curls the finger closed. Keeping the bulky muscle back in the forearm leaves the fingers slim enough to fit into tight spaces and move with fine control.

items.prompt: Why is it hard to lift your ring finger on its own while keeping the others flat on a table?

options.label: The ring finger has no muscle connected to it at all
options.feedback: The ring finger does have its own tendon pulling it; the difficulty is that this tendon is bound to its neighbours, not that it's missing.

options.label: The ring finger's bones are fused to the middle finger's bones
options.feedback: The bones of the fingers are entirely separate; nothing in the skeleton links them together.

options.label: The tendons that lift the fingers are cross-linked to each other, so pulling one tugs slightly on its neighbours
options.feedback: Thin bands of tissue connecting neighbouring tendons are exactly what causes that small shared tug.

options.label: It is purely a matter of practice, and enough training removes the limit completely
options.feedback: Practice can improve independent control somewhat, but the physical linkage between the tendons themselves stays whatever it is.

items.ok_line: A small physical link between the tendons causes the tug.
items.ko_line: The skeleton isn't the cause here, and practice alone can't remove a physical link between tendons.
items.exp_text: Each finger is lifted by its own tendon running across the back of the hand, but those tendons are not entirely separate cables — thin bands of tissue connect neighbouring ones to each other. Pulling on the ring finger's tendon to lift it also tugs, just slightly, on the tendons either side, and because the ring finger's own tendon is the weakest-anchored of the four, it is the one least able to move alone. That small shared tug is what makes it awkward to lift while its neighbours stay pinned down.

items.prompt: What does an opposable thumb let the hand do that would otherwise be impossible?

options.label: It lets the fingertip and thumb tip meet directly, forming a precise pinching grip
options.feedback: That direct fingertip-to-thumb contact is the specific trick a straight, unopposed thumb could never manage.

options.label: It makes the hand rotate all the way around at the wrist
options.feedback: The wrist, not the thumb, is what allows the hand to rotate; the thumb's special trick is something else entirely.

options.label: It simply makes the whole grip stronger
options.feedback: A thumb held straight against the palm can already add real force to a grip; the opposable thumb specifically buys precision, not raw strength.

options.label: It lets the thumb bend backward further than the fingers can
options.feedback: Extra backward bend isn't the trick, and most people's thumbs don't bend back further than their fingers do.

items.ok_line: Direct contact between thumb and fingertip is the whole trick.
items.ko_line: The opposable thumb's special contribution isn't strength or wrist rotation.
items.exp_title: A thumb that can meet its neighbours
items.exp_text: Most grasping animals can only close their fingers against the palm, the way a hand would clamp around a bar. A thumb that can swing across the palm to touch the tip of each finger adds a completely different kind of contact: a small, precise pinch between two fingertips, controlled independently of the rest of the hand. That pinch is what lets fingers do delicate work that a simple clamping grip never could.

items.prompt: What is the real difference between how you hold a hammer and how you hold a needle?

options.label: Both grips use exactly the same muscles; only the wrist angle differs
options.feedback: The two grips call on notably different sets of muscles, not just a different wrist tilt.

options.label: Holding a needle actually calls for more force than gripping a hammer
options.feedback: The opposite is closer to true; a hammer grip calls on far more force than the light contact needed to hold a needle steady.

options.label: The difference is only in which fingers touch the object, not which muscles act
options.feedback: Which fingers touch the object does change, but so does the whole system of muscles doing the work behind them.

options.label: A hammer is wrapped by the whole hand pressing into the palm, while a needle is held by a fingertip pinch using much smaller muscles
options.feedback: Whole-hand clamping and a fine fingertip pinch draw on two genuinely different sets of muscles.

items.ok_line: A whole-hand clamp and a fingertip pinch are built from different muscles.
items.ko_line: More than the wrist changes between these two grips.
items.exp_text: Wrapping the fingers and palm around a hammer's handle calls on the hand's strongest muscles, closing the whole hand into a solid clamp that channels force through the entire palm. Pinching a needle between fingertip and thumb uses a different, much smaller set of muscles inside the hand itself, built for light, precise contact rather than crushing force. The same hand switches between these two systems depending on what the task calls for.

items.prompt: What job do the tiny ridges on your fingertips do when you pick something up?

options.label: They increase the friction between skin and object, helping the fingers grip without slipping
options.feedback: Breaking up smooth contact and channelling away moisture is exactly how the ridges add grip.

options.label: They make the skin more flexible so it stretches around an object
options.feedback: Flexibility comes from the skin generally, not specifically from the ridged pattern; the ridges' job is elsewhere.

options.label: They reduce how much skin actually touches an object
options.feedback: The ridges do not shrink contact; if anything the raised parts increase the grip your skin gets on a surface.

options.label: They keep the fingertip cool while gripping
options.feedback: Cooling the skin is not something a ridge pattern does; that job belongs to blood flow and sweat, not to surface texture.

items.ok_line: The ridge pattern is what stops a slippery slide.
items.ko_line: The ridges aren't managing temperature or stretch; they're managing friction.
items.exp_title: Grip built into the skin's surface
items.exp_text: A perfectly smooth fingertip pressed against a smooth object has very little to stop it sliding, especially the moment any moisture gets between the two surfaces. The ridged pattern of a fingerprint breaks that smooth contact up, channelling moisture away and giving the raised ridges more direct purchase on the surface underneath. That extra purchase is what lets a slightly damp glass be held without it sliding out of the hand.

items.prompt: Why can the hand form so many different shapes, from a flat blade to a tight fist to a spread-out star?

options.label: The hand has a single very flexible bone that bends anywhere along its length
options.feedback: The hand's bones are individually rigid; the flexibility comes from many separate joints between them, not from one bendable bone.

options.label: Each finger has several small joints that can bend independently of one another, multiplying the possible shapes
options.feedback: Many independent small hinges, each bending to its own degree, is what produces such a wide range of shapes.

options.label: The skin of the hand is more elastic than skin elsewhere
options.feedback: Skin elasticity lets the surface stretch a little, but it is the underlying joints, not the skin, that actually let the fingers curl and spread.

options.label: Every finger shares one large joint at its base
options.feedback: Each finger has its own separate set of joints; there is no single shared joint doing the work of all of them.

items.ok_line: Independent joints, each with its own bend, multiply the possible shapes.
items.ko_title: Not the skin or one big bone
items.ko_line: Neither stretchy skin nor a single bendable bone explains this range of shapes.
items.exp_text: Each finger is not a single rigid piece but a chain of short bones connected by several small joints, and every one of those joints can bend to a different degree at the same time. With four fingers and a thumb each offering their own set of independent hinges, the combinations of how far each one bends add up to an enormous range of possible hand shapes. A flat blade, a closed fist and a spread star are simply different combinations of the same set of joints.

items.prompt: Why does the hand have small muscles packed between its own bones, when the forearm's larger muscles already supply plenty of power?

options.label: The small muscles inside the hand give fine, separate control over individual finger movements that the forearm's bigger muscles cannot provide alone
options.feedback: Separate, independent control of single fingers is exactly the job the forearm's shared tendons cannot manage on their own.

options.label: They exist mainly to keep the hand warm
options.feedback: Any warmth from small muscles working is a side effect, not their purpose; they exist for a job the more distant muscles cannot do as precisely.

options.label: They are leftover from an earlier stage of development and do little now
options.feedback: These muscles are active and doing real work every time the fingers move independently, not sitting unused.

options.label: They only add extra strength to what the forearm muscles are already doing
options.feedback: Their contribution is mostly about control and precision, not about adding raw pulling force to the forearm's larger effort.

items.ok_line: Fine, separate finger control is the job only these small muscles can do.
items.ko_line: These muscles are doing active, precise work, not sitting idle or keeping the hand warm.
items.exp_title: Control that has to live close by
items.exp_text: The forearm's big muscles pull on tendons that run down into the fingers, and mostly they pull several fingers together through shared connections, which is fine for closing the whole hand into a grip. Spreading the fingers apart, curling just one at a time, or making the tiny adjustments a precise pinch needs requires more separate, independent control than those shared tendons allow. The small muscles packed between the hand's own bones supply exactly that separate control, each one working a very specific, small movement.

items.prompt: Why is your grip noticeably weaker when your wrist is bent than when it is held straight?

options.label: A bent wrist cuts off blood flow to the fingers instantly
options.feedback: Normal wrist bending doesn't meaningfully block blood flow, and even if it did, that would take time to matter.

options.label: Bending the wrist shortens the fingers slightly
options.feedback: The bones of the fingers stay exactly the same length no matter what the wrist does.

options.label: Bending the wrist changes the angle the finger tendons pull at, so the same muscle effort produces less closing force
options.feedback: A tendon crossing a bent wrist is already partly used up getting around the bend, leaving less effective pull for the fingers.

options.label: A bent wrist sends a signal to the brain to relax the hand
options.feedback: There is no such signal; nothing about a bent wrist tells the brain to loosen the grip on purpose.

items.ok_title: A tendon at the wrong angle
items.ok_line: The tendon loses efficiency the moment the wrist bends.
items.ko_title: Not blood flow or a signal
items.ko_line: What weakens the grip is mechanical, not a circulation problem or a nerve signal.
items.exp_title: A tendon pulling at the wrong angle
items.exp_text: The tendons that curl the fingers closed run from the forearm, across the wrist, and into the fingers, and how much closing force they can deliver depends on the angle they cross that wrist at. Bend the wrist and those tendons are already partly used up just getting around the bend, leaving less travel and less effective pull left over for actually closing the fingers. Straightening the wrist lines the tendons up more directly, so the same muscle effort turns into a firmer grip.

items.prompt: Why does your hand develop a faint, fine tremor when you try to hold it perfectly still for a long stretch of time?

options.label: The hand tries to shake off dust settled on the skin
options.feedback: This has nothing to do with dust; the shake happens in a perfectly clean hand held over nothing at all.

options.label: Blood pressure spikes the longer the hand is held still
options.feedback: Blood pressure does not swing wildly just from holding a hand still; the tremor has a much more local cause.

options.label: The tendons stretch permanently longer under sustained tension
options.feedback: A tendon held under normal tension for a while does not permanently lengthen; it returns to its usual length once released.

options.label: Different small groups of muscle fibres take turns firing to share the load, and the tiny hand-offs between them show up as a faint shake
options.feedback: Those small, imperfect hand-offs between fibre groups are exactly what shows up as a fine tremor.

items.ok_line: The hand-off between fibre groups is what you're seeing as a shake.
items.ko_line: The tremor's cause is happening inside the working muscle itself.
items.exp_title: A relay race inside the muscle
items.exp_text: Holding a hand perfectly still is not really a single unbroken effort — it is made of many small bundles of muscle fibres, each one firing for a while and then resting while a neighbouring bundle takes over the load. As the effort goes on, some of those bundles begin to tire and hand off their share slightly less smoothly than at the start. Those small, imperfect hand-offs are what show up, magnified, as the fine shake in an outstretched hand.

items.prompt: What happens in your hand the instant an object you are holding starts to slip from your grip?

options.label: The hand releases the object completely to avoid dropping it further
options.feedback: Releasing would guarantee the drop; what actually happens is closer to the opposite, a quick tightening rather than letting go.

options.label: The grip tightens automatically and almost instantly, often before you consciously notice the slip
options.feedback: That fast, automatic correction is exactly what stops a slipping object from falling.

options.label: The other hand automatically reaches over to help
options.feedback: A single hand can and does correct a slipping grip entirely on its own; no second hand is required for this automatic response.

options.label: Nothing changes until you consciously decide to grip harder
options.feedback: Waiting for a conscious decision would usually be too slow; the correction happens faster than that.

items.ok_line: The correction is already underway before you've consciously noticed anything.
items.ko_title: Not release or a second hand
items.ko_line: A single hand corrects the slip on its own, and it does so by tightening, not letting go.
items.exp_title: A correction faster than a decision
items.exp_text: A grip is never held at one fixed, unchanging force — it is constantly being adjusted moment to moment to match how heavy and how slippery an object turns out to be. The instant an object begins to slide, that adjustment spikes sharply, tightening the grip in a fast, automatic correction. That correction is often already underway by the time a person becomes consciously aware that anything slipped at all.
